fissure.hero.title: Anal Fissure Treatment
fissure.hero.lede: A sudden sharp or burning pain when passing stool — the typical sign of an anal fissure. Many fissures heal with simple self-care; ones that last for weeks may need medical treatment.
fissure.what.p1: An anal fissure is a small tear in the lining of the anal canal — the short passage at the end of the bowel. The area is rich in nerve endings and the surrounding muscle tends to tighten in response to pain, so a fissure typically causes sharp pain during and after passing stool.
fissure.what.p2: Fissures are common and often heal with simple self-care. One that does not heal within a few weeks is called a chronic fissure and usually needs medical treatment. A long-standing fissure can leave a small skin tag beside the tear and can occasionally be linked to other conditions — so persistent symptoms deserve a proper examination.
fissure.symptoms.i1: Severe, sharp or burning pain when passing stool, which can continue for hours afterwards
fissure.symptoms.i2: Bright red blood on the toilet paper, on the stool surface or in the toilet water
fissure.symptoms.i3: A visible small tear or crack at the edge of the anus
fissure.symptoms.i4: Itching and irritation around the anus (more common in long-standing fissures)
fissure.symptoms.i5: A small skin tag at the end of a chronic fissure
fissure.symptoms.i6: Some people begin to avoid going to the toilet because of the pain — this can make constipation, and the fissure itself, worse
fissure.causes.p: Common causes and risk factors for an anal fissure:
fissure.causes.i1: Constipation and passing large or hard stools — the most common trigger
fissure.causes.i3: Reduced blood flow to the anal sphincter muscle — the tightened muscle limits healing
fissure.causes.i5: Inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis
fissure.causes.i7: Fissures are more common between the ages of 15 and 40, and in young children
fissure.when.i1: symptoms are not improving after about a week of self-care, or are getting worse
fissure.when.i2: any blood appears in the stool, in the toilet or on the toilet paper — bleeding has several possible causes and should not simply be assumed to be a fissure
fissure.when.i3: the pain makes you afraid to pass stool, or the pain comes with fever — this needs prompt assessment
fissure.when.p2: If the diagnosis is unclear or something more serious is suspected, the doctor may arrange a specialist examination.
fissure.treat.intro: The right treatment depends on how long the fissure has been present and how severe it is — your doctor will examine you and advise what is appropriate.
fissure.treat.home.d: Keep stools soft and easy to pass with plenty of fibre and fluids; warm, shallow baths (sitz baths) after passing stool ease the pain; paracetamol or ibuprofen can help if they are suitable for you; keep the area clean and dry — avoid straining and do not ignore the urge to go.
fissure.treat.med.d: Laxatives if constipation is present; creams or ointments that help the tear heal — these may need to be used for several weeks (up to around 8 weeks per NHS guidance); ointments that relax the anal muscle and improve local blood flow, such as diltiazem or nitroglycerin — on prescription; medicines to ease pain after passing stool, as advised by a doctor.
fissure.treat.clinic.d: An injection of botulinum toxin (Botox) into the anal muscle to relax the spasm so the tear can heal — a short procedure, usually done under anaesthesia.
fissure.treat.surg.d: Lateral internal sphincterotomy — a small cut is made in the internal anal muscle to reduce tension and improve blood supply, allowing the tear to heal. It is considered when other treatments have not worked or fissures keep coming back. As with any surgery, the benefits and risks — including a small risk of affecting bowel control — should be discussed with the surgeon.
fissure.treat.out: Your doctor will examine you and advise what is appropriate for you.
fissure.prevent.i1: Prevent constipation — a fibre-rich diet and plenty of fluids; add fibre gradually
fissure.prevent.i2: Do not delay going to the toilet, and do not strain
fissure.prevent.i3: Use a warm bath after bowel movements while the fissure heals
fissure.prevent.i4: Avoid harsh wiping; keep the area clean and dry
fissure.recov.p: Most acute fissures heal with simple self-care within a few weeks, although healing times vary. Chronic fissures often need prescribed ointments, Botox treatment or surgery, and healing after treatment can still take several weeks. Fissures can come back, especially if constipation continues — keeping stools soft is the key long-term habit. Your doctor will advise on follow-up if symptoms persist.
